title: Economic Survey 2025-26
source: Ministry of Finance, Government of India (January 2026)
note: Exam notes from the official Survey and Highlights PDF. Quote FAE numbers in Prelims; write trade-offs in Mains. Full PDFs download from S3 (signed link).

slides.caption: State of the economy — growth frontier

headlineNumbers.label: Potential growth (Survey)
headlineNumbers.hint: Revised up from 6.5% three years ago

howToUse: Prelims: memorise FAE 7.4% GDP, deficit path 9.2% (FY21) → 4.8% → 4.4% target, and ‘inflation tamed’ as the Survey’s own headline.
Mains GS-III: one paragraph on domestic demand + services, one on global tariff/geopolitics, one way-forward (reforms already named: GST overhaul, labour codes, nuclear/insurance FDI).
BPSC: add Bihar as an adaptation/agriculture/migration example; do not invent a Survey table for the state.
Never copy charts into the answer booklet — write the story the chart is telling.

chapters.title: State of the economy: pushing the growth frontier
points: FY26 First Advance Estimates: real GDP 7.4%, GVA 7.3%; growth is demand-led at home, services-led on the supply side.
Private consumption and capital formation are the two domestic engines; manufacturing has gained traction; agriculture is the stabilizer.
Survey revises India’s medium-term potential growth to 7.0% (from 6.5% three years ago).
Global backdrop: tariffs, fragmented supply chains, policy used as a strategic tool — India still prints strong macros.
Rupee ‘punches below its weight’: goods deficit + thinner capital flows even while inflation, banks and fiscal path look healthy.
chapters.exam: GS-III growth vs external shock. Pair with IMF WEO revisions, not newspaper panic.

chapters.title: Fiscal developments: credible consolidation
points: FY25 deficit 4.8% of GDP (budget 4.9%); FY26 target 4.4% — the 2021 promise to more than halve the FY21 9.2% deficit.
Three rating upgrades in 2025 (including S&P BBB- → BBB, first major-agency upgrade in nearly two decades).
GST collections tracking nominal GDP; quality of spending still the Mains question, not only the deficit ratio.
States’ finances and general-government debt sit in the same chapter — don’t write only the Union number.
chapters.exam: Prelims: 4.8 / 4.4 / 9.2 path. Mains: consolidation without cutting capex.

chapters.title: Monetary management and financial intermediation
points: RBI cut rates and eased liquidity as inflation and growth conditions allowed; 2023 macro-prudential tightness was later relaxed.
Banks’ books are described as healthy; credit growth ‘respectable’; corporate balance sheets strong.
Theme of the chapter: refine the regulatory touch — not deregulate blindly, not over-regulate MSME credit.
Global financial fragility (levered AI/data-centre SPVs, JGB yields) is the external risk to Indian markets.
chapters.exam: Repo vs Budget. Never assign GST cuts to the MPC.

chapters.title: External sector: playing the long game
points: Merchandise deficit vs services surplus + remittances is the BoP arithmetic; CAD stays manageable in the Survey’s telling.
US reciprocal + penal tariffs in 2025 were a shock; growth still accelerated — use this as a GS-II/III case of shock absorption.
Forex reserves remain the buffer; rupee underperformance is a capital-flow story as much as a trade story.
Long game: diversification of markets, services exports, and less dependence on a single destination.
chapters.exam: CAD, services exports, remittances, tariff shock. Bihar remittances as a household BoP.

chapters.title: Inflation: tamed and anchored
points: Survey headline: inflation is contained; food still drives the monthly noise (vegetables, TOP — tomato, onion, potato).
Core vs food is the MPC split: repo is blunt against a vegetable shock; buffers and logistics are the supply answer.
Regional/state inflation differences matter for BPSC/state answers — don’t quote only all-India CPI.
GDP deflator / manufacturing terms of trade is the advanced Prelims trap in this chapter.
chapters.exam: CPI vs WPI vs deflator. Who is hurt: wage lag, real rates, subsidy bill.

chapters.title: Agriculture and food management
points: Productivity + income + food security is the triad — not MSP alone.
Allied sectors and institutional interventions (not only the monsoon paragraph).
MSP, procurement of wheat/paddy, and food subsidy charts are in the Highlights PDF — know the direction, not 12 decimals.
Climate and water are the binding constraints; millets and diversification are the Survey-consistent way forward.
chapters.exam: GS-III agri. Bihar: floods, small holdings, horticulture.

chapters.title: Services: from stability to new frontiers
points: Services remain the largest GDP engine and the external-sector shock absorber (IT, travel, other business services).
New frontiers: digital, logistics, tourism, professional services — not only software exports.
Jobs test: services can grow without enough good jobs if informality stays high.

chapters.title: Industry’s next leap
points: Global manufacturing is shifting to high-tech value chains; India wants structural transformation, not only PLI slogans.
Core inputs (steel, chemicals, energy) plus MSME credit, competitiveness, and market access.
Labour codes notified — rules still the implementation paragraph.
QCOs paused where they hurt downstream industry: a deregulation example the Survey wants you to notice.
chapters.exam: PLI + MSME + logistics. Bihar’s thin factory base as contrast.

chapters.title: Investment and infrastructure
points: Capex, private participation, and multimodal connectivity (including inland waterways freight growth cited in the preface logic).
Energy + digital public infrastructure as ‘future-ready’ capex, not only roads.
Social infrastructure (health, education buildings) belongs here as well as in the human-development chapter.
chapters.exam: Gati Shakti flavour without dumping scheme logos.

chapters.title: Environment and climate
points: Adaptation and mitigation in one chapter: resilience + low-carbon competitiveness.
Climate finance and a lighter, growth-aware environmental regulation (green-cover norms differentiated by pollution potential).
Development-driven green transition — energy security is not optional in the Survey’s frame.
chapters.exam: NDC + just transition. Bihar = adaptation geography.

chapters.title: Education and health
points: Quality and access, not enrolment slogans. Learning outcomes are the Prelims/Mains hinge.
Public and preventive health over hospital-only thinking.
Human capital is why 7% potential growth can last — or not.
chapters.exam: ASER/NFHS style outcomes if you quote; else stay qualitative.

chapters.title: Employment and skilling
points: Getting skilling right is the chapter title — supply of certificates ≠ demand for tasks.
H1 FY26 labour-market charts: industry distribution and status (self-employed / casual / regular).
Youth skilling + job creation together; one without the other is a Mains fail.
chapters.exam: PLFS concepts. Migration from Bihar as the employment spillover.

chapters.title: Rural development and social progress
points: Poverty and inequality: ‘lifting millions’ plus the remaining last-mile.
From participation to partnership — SHGs, rural economy, social justice as inclusion enabler.
DBT and rural jobs schemes as governance, not as a slogan list.

chapters.title: AI ecosystem: the way forward
points: Development-oriented AI: public data, skills, safety — not only model-size nationalism.
Human capital and governance/data architecture are binding constraints.
Global AI capex leverage is a financial-stability footnote the preface already flagged.

chapters.title: Urbanisation
points: Cities lack economic agency (governance deficit).
Binding constraints: land, housing, mobility, sanitation/waste.
Informality is an urban outcome to integrate, not a stain to erase on paper.
Civic order needs a social contract — ethics overlap for GS-IV case studies.
chapters.exam: 74th CAA + services. Patna/urban Bihar as example.

chapters.title: Strategic resilience and indispensability
points: From import substitution nostalgia to strategic resilience: tiered indigenisation, input-cost reduction, advanced manufacturing as discipline.
State capacity is the binding constraint: culture, skills, execution, a capable regulatory state.
Compact of State + private sector + citizens. Swadeshi is framed as necessity in a harsher world, not as autarky.
Lowy ‘power gap’ mention in the preface: India operating below strategic potential — useful for GS-II IR.
